images.title: Endocrine Glands
images.caption: The endocrine glands release hormones straight into the blood. Crin/o means to secrete: endocrine glands secrete inward, into the blood, and exocrine glands secrete outward through ducts.
images.alt: Female and male body outlines showing the endocrine glands: pineal and pituitary glands in the brain, thyroid and parathyroid glands in the neck, adrenal glands on the kidneys, pancreas, ovaries and testes.
images.credit: OpenStax & Tomáš Kebert & umimeto.org, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Digestive Tract
images.caption: Food passes from the mouth through the pharynx, esophagus (Esophag/o) and stomach (Gastr/o) into the small intestine (Enter/o). The liver (Hepat/o), gallbladder and pancreas add digestive juices.
images.alt: Front view of the digestive system from the mouth to the rectum, showing the salivary glands, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine and appendix.
images.credit: Mariana Ruiz, Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Layers of the Skin
images.caption: Derm/o, Dermat/o and Cutane/o all mean skin. The epidermis is the outer layer, the dermis below it holds glands, hair follicles and nerves, and the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) stores fat.
images.alt: Cut-away block of skin showing the epidermis, dermis and hypodermis, with hair shafts and follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, arrector pili muscle, blood vessels, nerves and fat, and a hair follicle receptor.
images.credit: OpenStax College : J. Gordon Betts, Peter Desaix, Eddie Johnson, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Parts of a Cell
images.caption: Cyt/o means cell. The nucleus holds the genetic material, and the organelles in the cytoplasm make energy (mitochondria), build proteins (ribosomes, rough ER) and package them (Golgi apparatus).
images.alt: Cut-away drawing of an animal cell showing the nucleus, nucleolus, nuclear envelope, mitochondria, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosome, peroxisome, centrosome, secretory vesicle, cytoplasm and plasma membrane.

images.title: Structure of a Tooth
images.caption: Dent/o and Odont/o mean tooth, and Gingiv/o means gums. Hard enamel covers the crown, dentin forms the body of the tooth, and the pulp in the middle holds the nerves and blood vessels, which run down the root canal to the apex (the tip of the root).
images.alt: Cut-away of a molar in the jaw showing the enamel, dentin, pulp, root canal, gingiva and the root apex, with brackets marking the crown, neck and root.

images.title: Types of Permanent Teeth
images.caption: Adults have 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars (each jaw has 4 incisors, 2 canines, 4 premolars and 6 molars). Here each type has its own colour: incisors blue, canines yellow, premolars green, molars purple. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind food.
images.alt: Open mouth showing the upper and lower rows of permanent teeth, coloured by type: blue incisors, yellow canines, green premolars and purple molars.
images.credit: Gregory david baker, Vectorization:  Mrmw, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Bones of the Skull (Front View)
images.caption: Crani/o refers to the skull. The upper jaw is the maxilla and the lower jaw is the mandible, the only movable bone of the skull. The teeth are anchored in these two bones.
images.alt: Front view of the skull with each bone in a different colour: frontal, parietal, temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, nasal and zygomatic bones, the maxilla and the mandible.
images.credit: LadyofHats (Mariana Ruiz Villarreal), via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Bones of the Skull (Side View)
images.caption: From the side you can also see the occipital bone at the back of the skull. The temporal bone sits over the ear, and the zygomatic bone forms the cheek. Crani/o refers to the skull.
images.alt: Side view of the skull with each bone in a different colour: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, nasal and zygomatic bones, the maxilla and the mandible.
images.credit: LadyofHats (Mariana Ruiz Villarreal), via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Body Planes
images.caption: The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left parts, the coronal (frontal) plane into front and back, and the transverse plane into upper and lower parts. Here the three planes cross in the middle of the trunk.
images.alt: Standing figure cut by three see-through planes that cross at the waist: a red sagittal plane, a blue coronal plane and a green transverse plane.

images.title: Synovial Joint
images.caption: Arthr/o means joint and Chondr/o means cartilage. In a synovial joint, articular cartilage covers the bone ends, and synovial fluid inside the joint capsule lets the bones glide.
images.alt: Cross-section of a knee-type synovial joint showing the synovial cavity, joint capsule, articular cartilage, bursa, tendon, ligament, epiphyseal bone and the extensor and flexor muscles, with the proximal and distal bones marked.

images.title: The Human Skeleton
images.caption: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum) forms the body's central axis. The appendicular skeleton includes the limbs, shoulder girdle and pelvis. Oste/o means bone.
images.alt: Front view of the whole human skeleton with the skull, clavicle, scapula, sternum, ribs, humerus, vertebral column, ulna, radius, pelvis, femur, patella, tibia and fibula marked.
images.credit: LadyofHats (Mariana Ruiz Villarreal), via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Structure of a Long Bone
images.caption: A long bone has a shaft (diaphysis) and two ends (epiphyses). Hard compact bone forms the outer wall, while spongy bone fills the ends. The medullary cavity in the shaft holds bone marrow (Myel/o).
images.alt: A femur with one end cut open, showing spongy bone, compact bone and the medullary cavity, with brackets marking the epiphyses, metaphyses and diaphysis.

images.title: Body Planes and Sections
images.caption: The frontal (coronal) plane splits the body into front and back, the sagittal (median) plane into left and right, and the transverse (horizontal) plane into top and bottom.
images.alt: Three figures, each cut by one body plane, next to a matching section through the chest, the pelvis and the head.

images.title: Appendicular Skeleton
images.caption: The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that attach them: the shoulder girdle, the upper limbs, the pelvic girdle and the lower limbs.
images.alt: Skeleton with the limb bones and girdles highlighted, plus separate views of the shoulder girdle, the pelvic girdle and the limbs.

images.title: Axial Skeleton
images.caption: The axial skeleton is the body's central axis: the skull, the laryngeal skeleton, the vertebral column and the thoracic cage.
images.alt: Skeleton with the skull, spine and rib cage highlighted, plus separate views of the skull, the larynx cartilages, the spine and the rib cage.

images.title: Long Bones
images.caption: Long bones are longer than they are wide, like the bones of the arms, legs, hands and feet.
images.alt: An arm and a leg with the long bones marked, from the humerus and femur down to the phalanges.

images.title: Short Bones
images.caption: Short bones are about as wide as they are long. The carpals of the wrist and the tarsals of the ankle are short bones.
images.alt: A wrist and an ankle with the short bones highlighted.

images.title: Flat Bones
images.caption: Flat bones are thin and often curved. They protect organs and give muscles a broad place to attach.
images.alt: The skull, the rib cage, the sternum and a shoulder blade with the flat bones highlighted.

images.title: Irregular Bones
images.caption: Irregular bones have complex shapes that do not fit the other groups, such as the vertebrae and the sacrum.
images.alt: A spine with the vertebrae and the sacrum marked, next to a close view of the sacrum.

images.title: Sesamoid Bones
images.caption: A sesamoid bone sits inside a tendon. The patella (kneecap) is the largest one.
images.alt: Side view of the knee showing the patella inside the tendon at the front of the joint.

images.title: Heart Blood Flow Mind Map
images.caption: Blue blood from the body enters the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary valve to the lungs. Red blood comes back through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle and leaves through the aortic valve into the aorta. Cardi/o means heart.
images.alt: Animated mind-map style schematic of the heart: dots of blue blood flow from the body through the right atrium and right ventricle to the lungs, turn red, and return through the left atrium and left ventricle to the aorta and body. Four chambers and four valves are drawn. Dashed blue and red lines move along the vessels in the direction of flow.
images.credit: Study Portal drawing (adapted from the quiz's blood-flow animation)

images.title: Blood Flow Through the Heart
images.caption: The same route on a cutaway drawing of the heart. Deoxygenated (blue) blood from the vena cava fills the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle and leaves through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle and leaves through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the body tissues.
images.alt: Cutaway front view of a realistic heart diagram with its chambers, valves and great vessels, plus arrows for blood leaving to the lungs and to the body. All 14 labels are blank.
images.credit: Wapcaplet; no-labels version by Stenemo and Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons (leader lines, label boxes and flow arrows added)

images.title: Structures of the Heart
images.caption: The heart has four chambers (two atria and two ventricles) and four valves that keep blood flowing one way. The wall has three layers: endocardium, myocardium and epicardium.
images.alt: Cutaway front view of the heart showing its four chambers, valves, septa, great vessels and wall layers, with 21 blank labels connected to the structures by leader lines.
images.license: Course material (not openly licensed; internal course use only)
images.note: The labeled version is the original course image with the same crop.

images.title: Electrical Conduction System
images.caption: Each heartbeat starts at the SA node, the pacemaker. The signal passes to the AV node, then down the bundle of His and the bundle branches to the Purkinje fibers.
images.alt: Cutaway drawing of the heart with the conduction system highlighted: the SA node in the right atrium, internodal pathways, the AV node, the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers in the ventricle walls. The four chambers are also marked. All 11 labels are blank.
images.credit: Drj (CardioNetworks); blank version by YitzhakNat, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Coronary Arteries
images.caption: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself. A blockage in one of them causes a myocardial infarction (heart attack).
images.alt: Front view of the heart showing the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery with its branches on the heart's surface, along with the great vessels and chambers. All 14 labels are blank.
images.credit: Patrick J. Lynch, Fred the Oyster, Mikael Häggström, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Blood Vessels
images.caption: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it back. Gas exchange happens in the tiny capillaries between the arterioles and the venules. Angi/o and Vas/o mean vessel.
images.alt: Diagram of an artery carrying blood from the heart, branching into arterioles, a capillary network and venules, which join a vein that returns blood to the heart. Cutaways show the layers of the artery wall and a valve inside the vein, and a close-up of a capillary shows a red blood cell. All 13 labels are blank.
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Layers of the Heart Wall
images.caption: The heart wall has three layers: the outer epicardium, the thick muscular myocardium and the inner endocardium.
images.alt: A block cut from the heart wall showing its three layers, with a small heart for orientation.

images.title: Heart Valves
images.caption: The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between the atria and ventricles; the pulmonary and aortic valves guard the exits of the ventricles.
images.alt: A heart opened from above showing the four valves.

images.title: Blood Cells (Hematopoiesis)
images.caption: Hem/o and Hemat/o mean blood. Bone marrow makes erythrocytes (red cells), thrombocytes (platelets, from megakaryocytes) and leukocytes (white cells): neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes and lymphocytes.
images.alt: Family tree of blood cells formed in bone marrow, showing the erythrocyte, megakaryocyte and thrombocytes, the neutrophil, eosinophil and basophil, the monocyte and macrophage, and the lymphocytes (B and T cells, plasma cell and natural killer cell).
images.credit: A. Rad and Mikael Häggström, M.D. Author info - Reusing images- Conflicts of interest:  None, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Lymphatic System
images.caption: Lymph/o means lymph. Lymph vessels carry fluid back to the blood through the thoracic duct, and lymph nodes filter it along the way. The thymus (Thym/o) and spleen (Splen/o) are lymphatic organs.
images.alt: Female body outline with green lymph vessels and clusters of lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, abdomen, pelvis and groin, plus the thoracic duct, cisterna chyli, thymus and spleen.

images.title: Structure of a Lymph Node
images.caption: Lymph enters a node through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels. Inside, the cortex and medulla filter the lymph, and lymphocytes trap germs.
images.alt: Cut-away of a bean-shaped lymph node with afferent lymphatic vessels entering and efferent vessels leaving, showing the capsule, cortex, nodules, sinuses, medulla and valves.
images.credit: Lennert B (original); Tamil derivative by Commons user sibi, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Alveoli
images.caption: Alveol/o means air sac. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
images.alt: Close-up of grape-like clusters of alveoli at the end of a bronchiole, with the alveolar duct, alveolar sacs, pulmonary artery and vein branches and capillary beds around them.

images.title: Regions of the Pharynx
images.caption: The pharynx (throat, Pharyng/o) has three parts: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the mouth (Or/o), and the laryngopharynx above the larynx.
images.alt: Side view of the head cut down the middle, with the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx marked, plus the nasal cavity, hard palate and tongue.

images.title: The Respiratory Tract
images.caption: Air flows through the nasal cavity (Nas/o, Rhin/o), pharynx (Pharyng/o), larynx (Laryng/o) and trachea (Trache/o) into the bronchi (Bronch/o), which branch into the lungs (Pneum/o, Pulmon/o). The right lung has three lobes and the left has two.
images.alt: Front view of the respiratory system showing the nasal cavity, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, carina, right and left main bronchi, the three lobes of the right lung, the two lobes of the left lung, and the diaphragm.
images.credit: Bibi Saint-Pol, Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Respiratory System
images.caption: Air flows through the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea, then into the bronchi and bronchioles of the lungs.
images.alt: Head, neck and chest showing the airway from the nose down to the lungs.

images.title: Bronchioles and Alveoli
images.caption: Bronchioles are the smallest airways. They end in clusters of alveoli, the tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens.
images.alt: A lung with two boxed areas enlarged: a cut bronchiole and a cluster of alveoli wrapped in blood vessels.

images.title: Pharynx, Trachea and Esophagus
images.caption: The pharynx has three parts: the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx. Below it, air goes down the trachea and food down the esophagus.
images.alt: Side cut of the head and neck with the three parts of the pharynx shaded, and the trachea and esophagus below.

images.title: The Oral Cavity
images.caption: Looking into the mouth: the hard palate is the bony front of the roof, the soft palate is behind it, and the uvula hangs from it. The tonsils sit on each side.
images.alt: Photograph looking into an open mouth, showing the roof of the mouth, the uvula, the tonsils and the tongue.

images.title: Digestive System Structures
images.caption: Food passes from the oral cavity down the esophagus to the stomach, then the small and large intestines. The salivary glands, gall bladder and pancreas add digestive juices.
images.alt: Upper body showing the digestive tract from the mouth to the intestines.

images.title: Small Intestine
images.caption: The small intestine has three parts: the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. Its lining is covered in villi that absorb nutrients.
images.alt: Coils of the small intestine, with an enlarged piece of its lining showing the villi.

images.title: Large Intestine
images.caption: Chyme enters the cecum through the ileocecal valve, then moves through the ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon as it becomes feces. The appendix hangs from the cecum.
images.alt: The large intestine framing the abdomen, partly cut open to show its contents.

images.title: The Pancreas
images.caption: The main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct join and empty into the small intestine.
images.alt: The pancreas lying in the curve of the small intestine, with its duct and the bile duct cut open.

images.title: Liver, Gall Bladder and Duodenum
images.caption: The duodenum receives bile from the liver and gall bladder through the common bile duct, and juices from the pancreas through the pancreatic duct.
images.alt: The liver, gall bladder, stomach and pancreas around the first part of the small intestine.

images.title: Urinary System Structures
images.caption: Each kidney filters the blood and makes urine, which flows down a ureter to the bladder and leaves through the urethra.
images.alt: Two views of the urinary tract showing both kidneys, the ureters, the bladder and the urethra.

images.title: Inside the Kidney
images.caption: A cut kidney shows the outer cortex, the striped renal medulla and the renal pelvis that collects urine.
images.alt: A kidney cut in half lengthwise showing its inner regions.

images.title: Male Reproductive System
images.caption: Sperm form in the testicle, mature in the epididymis and travel through the vas deferens. The seminal vesicle, prostate and bulbourethral gland add fluid before it leaves through the urethra.
images.alt: Side cut of the male pelvis showing the reproductive organs.

images.title: Accessory Reproductive Glands
images.caption: The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands are the accessory glands that add fluid to sperm.
images.alt: Male reproductive organs with the accessory glands marked.

images.title: Pathway of Sperm
images.caption: Sperm travel from the testicle to the epididymis, up the vas deferens, through the ejaculatory duct into the prostatic urethra and out through the urethra.
images.alt: Male reproductive organs with arrows tracing the path of sperm.

images.title: Female Reproductive Structures
images.caption: The ovary releases an egg into the uterine tube, which leads to the uterus. The vagina connects the uterus to the vulva outside.
images.alt: Front cut of the female reproductive organs.

images.title: Embryo and Placenta
images.caption: The embryo grows inside its sac and is joined to the placenta by the umbilical cord.
images.alt: Photograph of an early embryo in its sac, attached by the umbilical cord to the placenta.
